lessons.title: The parts of a pig
lessons.html:
Why anatomy matters

To slaughter and dress a pig cleanly, you must know where the joints, organs and gut lie. This helps you cut without damaging the gut or valuable cuts, and helps you notice abnormalities for the meat inspector.

Digestive system

Unlike cattle, pigs have a single stomach (they are monogastric). Food goes down the oesophagus to the stomach, then through the small intestine and the large intestine (including the colon) to the rectum. The gut contents are full of germs, so the gut must not be cut during evisceration, and the rectum is freed and tied or bagged.

Organs

OrganWhere
Heart, lungs, windpipeChest cavity (together called the pluck, with the liver in some plants)
DiaphragmBetween chest and belly
Liver (with gall bladder)Front of the belly, against the diaphragm
Stomach and spleenLeft front of the belly
IntestinesMost of the belly cavity
KidneysUnder the loin, in the leaf fat
Bladder and reproductive organsPelvis

Lymph nodes

Lymph nodes are small glands found in the head, neck, around organs and in the carcass. The meat inspector cuts and checks some of them because they show signs of infection. Do not cut or remove them before inspection unless your procedure says so.

The carcass and its cuts

The pork carcass includes the skin, back fat, and the main cuts: shoulder, loin (with the chops), belly (for bacon) and leg (for ham). The splitting saw runs down the middle of the backbone. Careless knife work or bruises on the loin and leg lower the value of the carcass.

lessons.title: Recognising abnormalities in pigs
lessons.html:
Notice and report

Your job is to notice abnormalities and report them. Only the meat inspector decides whether a carcass or organ is passed, trimmed or condemned. Keep the carcass, head and offal together and identified until inspection is complete.

Common abnormalities

AbnormalityWhat you see
Pork measles (cysticercosis)Small, fluid-filled whitish cysts in the muscles, tongue and heart. Caused by a tapeworm that can cause serious illness in people. Report at once.
Milk spot liverWhite spots on the liver from migrating roundworms
Pneumonia and pleurisyDark, firm areas in the lungs; lungs stuck to the ribs
AbscessesPockets of pus, for example from tail biting or injections. Do not cut into them.
ErysipelasRaised, diamond-shaped red patches on the skin; swollen joints
ArthritisSwollen, inflamed joints
Bruises and bite woundsBloody areas from fighting or rough handling
HerniasSwellings at the navel or groin, which may contain gut; take great care when cutting
JaundiceYellow fat and tissues
PSE / DFD meatPale, soft, watery meat, or dark, firm, dry meat, linked to stress
Unusual reddening or bleeding of skin and organsCan be a sign of a serious disease such as African swine fever; report immediately

What to do

  1. Stop and call the meat inspector.
  2. Do not continue processing the affected parts.
  3. If you cut into pus or a cyst, sterilise your knife and wash your hands and arms.
  4. Wear gloves; some pig diseases can infect people.

Key points

  • Pigs have a single stomach; the gut must not be cut.
  • Know where the organs and lymph nodes are.
  • Pork measles can infect people: report it at once.
  • Common abnormalities include milk spot liver, pneumonia, abscesses and erysipelas.
  • Only the meat inspector decides; keep carcass, head and offal together.
